newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Meyer sees risk of higher U.S. inflation.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Meyer sees risk of higher U.S. inflation.

text.p: Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer on Thursday forecast near-trend growth for the U.S. economy this year but saw a risk of higher inflation.

"Recent data have not altered my expectation that the economy will grow near trend over the next year," he said in a speech for delivery to the Economics Club here, adding he saw little sign of imbalances that would endanger the upswing.
But, he added, "I have slightly greater concern that inflation will increase than that the economy will lapse into persistent, below-trend growth and face rising unemployment."
The U.S. central bank thus must watch carefully for signs of growing price pressures and act quickly if needed to contain them.

"The challenge is to be especially watchful for early signs of mounting price pressures and, if necessary, to be at least swiftly reactive to limit and then reverse any acceleration of inflation that might occur," he said.
Meyer said core inflation may rise gradually in 1997. But the overall rate may drop, due to slower rises in food prices and a partial reversal of the recent run-up in energy prices.
Meyer spent much of his speech discussing the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU) and whether, by how much and for how long, it had fallen.
"There remains some uncertainty as to whether the current unemployment rate will prove consistent with stable inflation over time," he said. "It would be unwise to ignore this risk."

The unemployment rate in December stood at 5.3 percent, well below the six percent rate most economists thought constituted full employment just a few years ago. But underlying inflation has not increased.
Meyer said that the uncertainty over NAIRU has made the Fed more cautious in carrying out interest rate policy.
"Forward-looking policy is predicated on confidence in a model that can predict how current and prospective economic conditions will affect inflation going forward," Meyer said.

"Uncertainty about NAIRU has, in my view, made monetary policy more cautious in responding to forecasts of inflation that depend on the relationship between the current unemployment rate and some estimate of NAIRU," he said.
However, if unemployment falls, that could change.
"If the unemployment rate declines ... a more forward-looking approach may quickly become appropriate," Meyer said.
He said that some of the recent apparent drop in the NAIRU was likely transitory because it had come about from a series of temporary, favorable supply shocks.
Among those "shocks": lower health care costs, a rapid decline in computer prices and lower import prices stemming from the rise of the dollar and lower inflation abroad.

Discussing some of the reasons the NAIRU may have fallen, Meyer said some of it may be tied to a greater feeling of uncertainty among U.S. workers that has made them less likely to demand higher wages.
He said an apparent increase compared to the 1980s in workers suffering permanent job losses was one piece of evidence supporting this view.
Also, there appear to be signs that workers are less willing to leave their jobs because of fear they might not find new ones, he said.
Aside from worker insecurity, some economists have linked a decline in the NAIRU to firms' difficulty in raising prices due to increased competition.
However, Meyer tended to dismiss that argument, saying, "The absence of pricing leverage may simply reflect the fact that product markets are not tight, compared to labor markets."
